title: 1 Chronicles 10:8–14
context: The Philistines strip the dead, take Saul’s head and armor, and send the news to their idols and people, placing his armor in the house of their gods and fastening his head in the house of Dagon. The valiant men of Jabesh Gilead recover the bodies of Saul and his sons, bury the bones under the oak in Jabesh, and fast seven days. The Chronicler then gives his own verdict: Saul died for his trespass against the LORD, for not keeping the LORD’s word and for consulting a medium instead of inquiring of the LORD, so the LORD turned the kingdom over to David. The parallel is 1 Samuel 31:8–13, which differs in several details (Beth Shan and the Ashtaroth, the burning of the bodies, and a tamarisk rather than an oak); these differences are noted rather than resolved.

verses.text: On the next day, when the Philistines came to strip the slain, they found Saul and his sons fallen on Mount Gilboa.
verses.arminianNotes: The next day the Philistines find Saul and his sons on Mount Gilboa. Arminian readers note the bleak scene of victors stripping the dead, a reminder of the humiliation that defeat brought to Israel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the discovery as the start of the dishonor done to Saul’s body. Both traditions read the verse as parallel to 1 Samuel 31:8, where Samuel specifies “his three sons” and Chronicles says “his sons.”

verses.text: They stripped him and took his head and his armor, then sent into the land of the Philistines all around to carry the news to their idols and to the people.
verses.arminianNotes: The Philistines strip Saul, take his head and armor, and send the news to their idols and people. Arminian readers note that the victory is celebrated as a triumph of the Philistine gods over Israel’s king.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the boast before idols as an affront to the LORD that will later be answered. Shared ground: the verse parallels 1 Samuel 31:9, and both traditions read it soberly without dwelling on the treatment of the body.

verses.text: They put his armor in the house of their gods, and fastened his head in the house of Dagon.
verses.arminianNotes: They put Saul’s armor in the house of their gods and fasten his head in the house of Dagon. Arminian readers note that 1 Samuel 31:10 mentions the house of the Ashtaroth and the wall of Beth Shan instead.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the mention of Dagon, whose temple had earlier been humbled before the ark (1 Samuel 5:1–5). Both traditions note the differences from Samuel without resolving them, and read the verse as describing dishonor done to Saul.

verses.text: When all Jabesh Gilead heard all that the Philistines had done to Saul,
verses.arminianNotes: All Jabesh Gilead hears what the Philistines have done to Saul. Arminian readers note that the men of Jabesh remember Saul’s earlier rescue of their city (1 Samuel 11:1–11) and respond with gratitude.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see loyalty to the LORD’s anointed even in death. Shared ground: the verse parallels 1 Samuel 31:11, and both traditions read it as the start of a courageous act of honor, as the 1 Samuel notes also do.

verses.text: all the valiant men arose and took away the body of Saul and the bodies of his sons, and brought them to Jabesh, and buried their bones under the oak in Jabesh, and fasted seven days.
verses.arminianNotes: The valiant men take the bodies of Saul and his sons to Jabesh, bury their bones under the oak, and fast seven days. Arminian readers note the courage and devotion shown in honoring the dead.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see dignity restored in burial and mourning. Both traditions note that 1 Samuel 31:12–13 mentions burning the bodies and a tamarisk tree, while Chronicles mentions an oak and no burning; the difference is noted, not resolved.

verses.text: So Saul died for his trespass which he committed against the LORD, because of the LORD’s word, which he didn’t keep, and also because he asked counsel of one who had a familiar spirit, to inquire,
verses.arminianNotes: The Chronicler says Saul died for his trespass: he did not keep the LORD’s word and consulted a medium (1 Samuel 28:7–19). Arminian readers see the verdict as tied to Saul’s own choices of disobedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s just judgment on a king who turned from the LORD’s word. Shared ground: both traditions accept the Chronicler’s verdict as stated, and neither forces a contrast over it; it is a theological summary of Saul’s reign.

verses.text: and didn’t inquire of the LORD. Therefore he killed him, and turned the kingdom over to David the son of Jesse.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul did not inquire of the LORD, so the LORD killed him and turned the kingdom to David. Arminian readers note that 1 Samuel 28:6 says Saul inquired and received no answer; the two statements are noted without harmonizing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the Chronicler attributing Saul’s death ultimately to the LORD, who gives the kingdom to David. Both traditions read the verse as the Chronicler’s interpretation, which frames the rest of the book around David’s line.
